question_en: A T-bill with 121 days to maturity has a 360-day assumed year and a USD 1 million par value. If it is currently priced at USD 988,176, then its discount rate is closest to:
explanation_en:
A money market interest rate is expressed as either a discount rate or an add-on rate. Both are annualized rates. A discount rate is a percentage
of the future value (ie, par value) of the instrument; it applies to money market investments sold at a discount. An add-on rate is a percentage of
the bond's present value or price. The discount rate of a money market instrument is calculated as the change in value (FV − PV) divided by
future value. The rate is annualized by multiplying it by the instrument's periodicity (days in the year ÷ days in the period).
In this scenario, the days in the period are equal to the days until maturity. The money market discount rate is calculated as:
Unlike a bond market discount rate or a yield to maturity, which are each percentages of a present value, a money market discount rate is a
percentage of a future value, annualized by multiplying the change in value (FV − PV) by the periodicity. In contrast, investors measure their rate
of return as a percentage of the amount being invested. This means that the money market discount rate understates the investor's rate of return,
which is a percentage of the present value, not the future value.
(Choice A) 1.18% results from not annualizing the rate. After determining (FV − PV) ÷ FV, multiply by (days in the year ÷ days until maturity),
using the correct year convention (ie, 360 or 365). This will determine the correct annualized discount rate.
(Choice C) 3.56% results from dividing by the present value to find the periodic interest rate. This is the equivalent of calculating an add-on rate.
Discount rates for money market instruments are calculated by dividing by the instrument's future value, not its present value.

explanation_en:
A floating-rate note (FRN) is a debt instrument with an interest rate that resets periodically, so that the interest rate and payments are "floating" and
not fixed. The interest rate is based on a reference rate, such as LIBOR, plus a quoted margin, which compensates the investor for the credit risk
of the issuer.
The price of an FRN is its discounted future payments, where the discount factor is based on the reference rate plus a discount margin. The
discount margin represents the market's required spread to price the FRN at par on the reset date.
To solve for the discount margin, first calculate the discount factor and then use that to derive the discount margin.

question_en: Of the following, the government equivalent yield best describes yield to maturity (YTM):
option_a: restated from a 30/360 day-count basis to an actual/actual day-count basis.
option_b: calculated based on the actual dates that the bond pays interest and principal.
option_c: calculated by assuming that interest and principal are paid on their scheduled dates.
explanation_en:
A bond's yield describes and quantifies its return. One yield measure used for corporate bonds is the government equivalent yield. Many
corporate bonds use a 30/360 day-count convention, whereas government bonds, particularly US Treasury notes and bonds, use an actual/actual
day-count convention. Each bond's YTM is based on its day-count convention, so the yields cannot be directly compared.
The government equivalent yield results from converting a corporate bond's YTM, which is based on a 30/360-day basis, to the YTM based on the
actual/actual basis of a government bond. This makes the yields directly comparable and shows the additional yield required to compensate
investors for the corporate bond's additional risk.
(Choice B) The true yield is similar to the yield obtained from using the street convention but is modified to account for the actual day that a
payment occurs (eg, an interest payment scheduled for a Sunday is instead made on the following Monday).
(Choice C) The street convention is a bond's YTM calculated under the assumption that all payments are made on their scheduled dates,
regardless of whether a scheduled date is a trading day.

question_en: A floating-rate note will most likely be priced at a premium when the quoted margin is:
explanation_en:
Floating-rate notes (FRN [ie, floaters]) are debt instruments that make interest (coupon) payments based on a reference rate, which can fluctuate
from one period to the next. The reference rate is typically a short-term, low-risk money market rate, such as LIBOR.
Since FRN investors may face additional credit risk, a quoted yield spread (ie, quoted margin) is added to the reference rate to compensate for
this risk. The discount margin (ie, required margin) reflects investor return expectations and is used for discounting future interest payments to the
present value of the FRN.
An FRN will trade at a premium if the quoted margin that the issuer pays is greater than the required margin that the market demands. This is
similar to a fixed-rate bond, which sells at a premium when the coupon rate is greater than its YTM.
(Choice A) The FRN will trade at a discount, not premium, when the quoted margin is less than the discount margin.
(Choice B) The size of the quoted margin relative to the reference rate has no bearing on whether an FRN trades at a premium or discount.

addition to the reference rate required to compensate bondholders for the bond's credit risk such that the bond would be priced at par. If the

at par on its reset date. If the required margin is greater than the quoted margin, the note will be priced at a discount since the coupon payments

question_en: The forward curve consists of the following rates, which are stated on a semiannual basis: Based on this information, the implied three-year spot rate is closest to:
explanation_en: The implied forward rate (or just "forward rate") is an interest rate derived from the current zero-coupon bond term structure (ie, spot curve). Arbitrage-free pricing enforces the consistency of forward rates with spot rate differences. A forward rate can be interpreted as the incremental return required for extending the time-to-maturity by an additional period. For example, in this scenario an investor would be indifferent to investing in a three-year zero-coupon bond at 2.15% or investing in a two-year zero-coupon bond at 1.85% and then, two years from now, in a one-year zero-coupon bond at 2.75% (ie, the "2y1y" forward rate), since both result in the same return in three years. The implied forward rate is the breakeven reinvestment rate required to make the two transactions equivalent. If an investor believes that the one-year rate two years in the future will be lower than the breakeven rate of 2.75%, the investor is better off buying the three-year zero-coupon bond today. (Choice A) The implied spot rate of a two-year zero-coupon bond in one year is quoted as 1y2y, not 2y1y. (Choice B) The rate of return of the three-year zero-coupon bond is known (ie, 2.15%); it is the return of the one-year zero-coupon bond in two years that is uncertain. The implied forward rate is the required rate of return for the investor to be indifferent to the two transactions.

Yield curves are ideally constructed using bonds with the same characteristics, such as maturity, coupon rate and frequency, credit risk,
liquidity, tax status, etc. It is unlikely that bonds fitting all these criteria will be readily available, so the most practical solution is to create a spot
curve using a series of government zero-coupon bonds with various maturities.
This is the preferred solution since these bonds have many common features: the same issuer, liquidity, and tax status. Since they are
government bonds, they are assumed to have no default risk and as zero-coupon bonds, they have no reinvestment risk.
Note that bonds issued by any government always have some risk of default and that some sovereign issuers are riskier than others, but it is
generally assumed that bonds issued by governments of certain nations are effectively free of default risk.
(Choice A) A par curve is designed so that the bonds represented by the YTMs at every point of the curve are priced at par. This assumption
does not apply to spot curves.
(Choice B) A spot curve is compiled using YTMs of zero-coupon government bonds.

question_en: A benchmark government yield curve is most likely obtained from:
explanation_en:
Yield curves display the term structure of interest rates by graphing the relationship between maturities and bond yields. Government bonds form
the basis of most yield curves, the most fundamental of which is the yield curve on coupon bonds (ie, the coupon curve).
Many governments regularly issue bonds in select maturities such as 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, and 30 years, and these bonds form the backbone of the
"benchmark" coupon curve. As government coupon curves are constructed using only the most recently issued and actively traded bonds as
benchmarks, the remainder of the curve is constructed using interpolation (ie, estimated values) to connect these points.
(Choices B and C) The spot curve is constructed from a series of government zero-coupon bonds of different maturities. A par curve is
constructed from a spot curve and represents the coupon rate for a given maturity such that the bond would trade at par when each coupon
payment is discounted by the appropriate term spot rate. Spot and/or par curves are not used to construct a benchmark coupon curve.
